utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Di Fazio, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Antic? MR. DI FAZIO: I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Antic, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please speak as close to the microphone as possible. Mr. Di Fazio, please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter]l Examination by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, yesterday I was asking you some questions about your personal details, your background. In -- no, I want to ask you now about the village you lived in in 1998; that was named Locane, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's located fairly close to Decani, slightly to --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Decani, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just wait for me to finish my questions. And it's located slightly to the west, I think, of the Decani-Djakovica road. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the direction of Decani and Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. I want you to give the Trial Chamber an idea of the demography of the village, the population that lived there. Can you tell us how many Serbs -- households and Serbs lived in Locane in early 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were five Serb households, Serb. Albanian, near 200 households.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you remember any of the names of the Serbs who lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have them, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simic Jordan; Simic Svetozar; Danilovic Djordje; Danilovic Ilija; Danilovic Vuko; Simic Svetozar; Dvaljevic [phoen] Spasoje; Antic Slavoljub; Antic Dasko; Antic Djordje --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to pause there. I'm terribly sorry. I think -- I think it was my fault. I think I misled you. All I was really asking for was the family names of the Serbs, not the name of each individual, otherwise we'll be here a long time. So what were the main family names of the Serbs living in your village?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Antic, Simic, Danilovic, and the house near the elementary school building near the Slup, Glovarevic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Fine. That's good enough a picture. Thank you. In early 1998 before April, were you commuting from your house or your home in Locane to your work in Decani?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the way up until April, until we left the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And at this time, you were engaged in full-time duties as a policeman in your capacity as a reserve policeman. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not throughout. Only when the situation was tense. It was then that they called me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was asking you a little bit about this yesterday and I'm still not quite sure. What I'd like you to do is tell the Trial Chamber as clearly as you can how your day-to-day activities were conducted in the first three months of 1998: January, February, March. Now, were you going to the police station and doing policeman's jobs every single day, or were you also sometimes also going to your civilian work? Was it a combination of one or the other? Can you describe it to the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ever since 1990, I had been with the reserve police, and at those times I was not with the factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what about early 1998, those three months, did you do mainly police work in those three months, or were you doing mainly work at the factory, or was it a combination of both?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you eventually take a -- did you eventually leave Locane?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1998, the day after Easter day when the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just give me a moment to transfer to this other microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask, for my orientation, what religion do you belong to and if this Easter is the Orthodox Easter you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Orthodox Easter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say you made -- you took your decision the day after Easter when the shooting started. Firstly, did you take your family with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My two sons and my wife; my father refused to leave. He was an old man, 61 or 62 at the time. He said, I'm an old man. Take your family and go to your father-in-law's house in Pec, because that was a safer place to be at the time. I followed suit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your father is Ilija Antic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you, in fact, take up -- leave your house and go and take up residence in Pec in your father-in-law's house?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now some questions concerning the reason for your departure. Now, you've already started to touch upon that because you mentioned that you took your decision the day after Easter when the shooting started. Now, what -- what was going through your mind as to the reason why you should leave your village where you lived and go to Pec? What were you worried about? What were you concerned about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I was wounded when I left the village of Locane, my father remained in the village. I would go back every so often to bring him food and cigarettes. I saw all the people there, but I recognised none. There was this one time I was on my way back just past midnight, and at the bridge I met six men wearing black uniforms. I told them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And then the witness says something in Albanian which the interpreter didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and they didn't reply. They crossed the bridge, and they went straight to their HQ where the late Vida had been killed and that's where the HQ was. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But just think very carefully -- I'll ask you some more questions about what you've told us in a moment, but think carefully about my question. You said that you left the day after -- you left your house and your village with your family, your wife and kids, and you left the day after Easter. Firstly, did your decision have anything to do with this shooting that you have referred to? Just answer me yes or no. Did that play a part in your decision to leave your village?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only because of the shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So you took your decision the day after Easter, so then -- am I correct then that the shooting occurred at some point before the day after Easter? Just answer me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, will you please tell the Trial Chamber what shooting you are referring to, when you heard it or saw it, where it occurred, and who was doing the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had been sleeping in my room. It was about 9.00. My wife came, my father came, they'd been outside, and the shooting was coming from Prilep, the direction of Prilep or possibly Drenovac. All of those were illumination bullets. All those with families left. Only the elderly remained behind. All of those with families left for Decani for the sake of our family's safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say illumination bullets, are you refer to tracer bullets, bullets that leave a trace after they've been fired from a gun?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, tracer bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you then said that having heard of -- heard the shooting from Prilep and having seen these tracer bullets, you then went on to say that: All those with families left and only the old people remained. Can you -- just a minute. Just a minute, wait for the question. Remember just to wait for the question, and then you'll find it a lot easier to answer. And then you went -- then you said all of those families left for Decani. Now, what I would like you to explain to the Trial Chamber is this: Was that a decision that a number of families took at the one time, or did it happen that families left for Decani in dribs and drabs slowly over the next few days, or was there a mass -- not a mass, but a large movement of families, Serbs, from your village?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother Miodrag Antic, he left two days, his family, and he stayed with his father and mother. Slavoljub Antic, my brother too, left with our mother and his family for Decani. Jordan Simic did the same thing with his family, he left. His mother and aunt remained behind. Vuk Danilovic and Ilija Danilovic followed this example, too; as well as Svetozar Simic with his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. Thank you for explaining that. Now, can I ask you this: Of those people you say who actually left the village, did they all leave at about the same time, or did it happen over a period of days or longer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them one day and the other the next day. They didn't leave altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And -- using the day after Easter as a marking point, can you say if they left both before and after that day, or was it only after that day that they left?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's who I've been talking about, yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all left the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Can you tell us if you all left the same day after Easter or did some leave before and some after?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miodrag Antic, his wife took the children and left, she did. After her, Slavoljub Antic left too, so did Svetozar Simic, Jordan Simic. My wife and I left the last day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, earlier I was asking you some questions about your reasons for leaving. You mentioned the -- the firing that you could hear from Prilep and the tracer bullets, and you also started to mention an episode where you were with some men on a bridge. Can you now tell the Trial Chamber what the episode -- what the episode was you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise for rising, but it might be helpful to clarify whether this episode took place before or after the witness left because the way in which I'd heard the evidence may not be quite the same as the way in which Mr. Di Fazio heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, I would like to have clarified one issue. Mr. Di Fazio, any objection to follow the suggestion made by Mr. -- MR. DI FAZIO: No, no; in fact, I fully intend to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Antic, you at one moment said one of them left on one day and the other the next day. They didn't leave altogether. A few lines further down, you said: We all left the same day. Were you referring the first time to the Serbs, that means the families, all of them, one one day, another the other day; and the second time to your own family? Or have I misunderstood this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it's correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- what I said is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and my understanding was correct as well, as far as I understand. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try and get a time on this episode at the bridge that you referred to first before I ask you about it. You did refer to an episode on a bridge with some men. Now, can you tell us when that took place, before or after you left your village?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That took place in April, the 20th of April. I was on my way to visit my father, to bring him food and cigarettes, and I came across five or six of them in black uniforms. However, they were not armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So I take it -- am I correct that this episode with the men on the bridge, when you were going to visit your father, took place after you had taken your -- made your decision to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to return now to the firing that you could see from -- see and hear from the direction of Prilep. Why did that cause you concern so that you left your village? Why -- what was it about that, that had you worried?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every night they were arming themselves; every night there were lorries and tractors going towards Voksa and Junik. There was noise throughout the night produced by cars, lorries, and tractors, and that's why all of us Serbs decided to leave the area. Only the elderly remained in their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we're going to need a lot more detail about the people you referred to as they. You say "they were arming themselves" and there was lorries and tractors. Now, who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, think about it. Civilians. What sort of civilians? Men? Women? Children? Adults? What ethnicity? Can you give us some information about them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The young went, aged between 20 and 40, not the women, though, or the children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question, Mr. Antic. You said to the Trial Chamber that - and listen carefully, please listen very carefully - you said this: "Every night they were arming themselves, every night there were lorries and tractors going towards Voksa and Junik ... noise throughout the night produced by cars, lorries, and tractors ..." Now, it's a very simple question. When you say: "Every night they were arming themselves ...", can you provide any information as to who "they" were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their names, if that's what you mean. There was noise just before Easter and we couldn't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm not asking for names, but could you give us a description of who these people were, any sort of description? And of course if you never saw them or got no idea at all, please tell the Trial Chamber and we'll move on. I'm not trying to suggest that you know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them. We just heard the noise, that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you heard noises, and for that reason you decided to leave your village. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what was it about these noises that so troubled you -- I'll withdraw that question? What Serbs remained -- did -- you said only the elderly remained in your village of Locane. Can you remember any of their names, apart from your father, Ilija Antic, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean out of the Serbs who remained behind in Locane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. Yeah?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My late father, Ilija, remained; as well as my uncle Djordje; his wife, Milosava; my cousin on the uncle's side remained there for another three to four days and then went back to Decani and remained there; Vidosava Simic stayed there, as well, with his sister Borka. That's it, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell can the Trial Chamber if you noticed any corresponding movement amongst the Albanian families that lived in your village? Did they also go and take up residence in towns in the area?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not. When I went to visit my father, he told me that there were women coming from elsewhere, from Glodjane, Rznica, and from some other areas. And he said that there were men he didn't know because they were not the inhabitants of our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give you any information as to the ethnicity of these people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanians. MR. DI FAZIO: Can we go into private session very briefly, if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to continue asking you some questions about this man whose name you mentioned in private session. Did you have a chance to see him in late 1997/early 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a policeman, a professional policeman. He worked as a traffic policeman in Istok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if he was a member of any organisation in 1997 or 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I only know that I used to see him with some young people training them. They would run at night since there was a wooded area just above the village, and they used to run there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was he a keen athlete? Did he have a running club - do I understand you correctly - or was there some other activity going on? If you could just clarify.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose they were preparing themselves for war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Antic, have you got any reason for making that supposition?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was training people daily and at night, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I understand that, and you suppose that they were preparing themselves for war, and you mentioned the training. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But my question is not whether they were training, but how you know what they -- how do you know what they were doing? Did you see it with your own eyes? Did you receive information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw them myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At night or during the day or both?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the day, but at dusk I would see 10 to 15 of them running through the forest and he headed the group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I still haven't really received an answer to an earlier question, and I'd like to ask it again. You said you suppose that they were preparing themselves for war, and I asked you if you had any reason and you referred to training. And you've just again mentioned seeing them running. Now, what is it about their running that made you think that they were preparing for war, or did you observe something else apart from running?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would assemble every night. They would meet and discuss what and how to do things. They discussed digging trenches and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you know that? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one goes to the village cemetery in Locane, my neighbours told me that they saw three men digging trenches at Carove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that somehow related to the man whose name we mentioned in private session or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but I didn't see him. It is possible that it was his school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to another topic now. On the 25th of May, 1998, Mr. Antic, were you -- were you driving to work?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about what happened to you on that day, but before I do, can I ask you this: As far as you were aware, was your father, Ilija Antic, still alive on that day, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Can you tell me who else was in your vehicle, if anyone -- if anyone?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me the names of the people who were in your car?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a fellow policeman there, he was new to the police and I don't know what his name was. There was a driver there as well. He worked with the utility company, the electricity company, in Decani. His nickname is Striko. There was also an old man from Dasinovci. I think his first name was Dimitrije; I don't know his last name. It may be that he was Dimitrije Popovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a policeman as well, this Dimitrije?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was an elderly person, a civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The car you were travelling in, whose vehicle was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The car belonged to the driver who worked for the electricity company. It was not an official car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you dressed in uniform or were any of the other occupants in the car dressed in uniform, police uniform, or indeed any soldiers or military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The colleague of mine was there. He was in the co-driver's seat. He had the uniform on, as well as I did, and we went to relieve the previous shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Police uniform, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, it's -- I don't think it's in dispute in this case. Can you tell us how -- how you were shot at and what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened on the 25th of May. It was five minutes to 7.00. We arrived at Ljubenic where the bus station was. Some 100 metres before the station, there is a curve onto a road. They were standing there with 20 metres between each of them, and as soon as they saw us in uniform they opened fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was there any attempt to stop you or the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no attempt to stop us. As soon as they saw our uniforms, they opened fire. It was our luck that they were young and they couldn't handle their weapons properly. They opened fire at us and turned their heads the other way at the same time. Dimitrije was injured; he got a bullet to one of his muscles. And they hit me below the knee with a dum-dum, an explosive-charge bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you if you can tell us who "they" are? Have you got any details about "they," then the Trial Chamber would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Ramush Haradinaj's army. They wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well -- okay. First of all, can you remember how many of these men wearing camouflage uniforms there were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I suppose events must have happened fairly fast, and if you can't remember, I don't want you to provide details, only if you can remember. Can you tell us if they were all armed, or only some of them, or you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all armed. There was a canal next to the road on the right-hand side. When two of them saw that the car kept moving, they came out of the canal. Our driver saw him and hit him with the right-hand side of the car, throwing him back down. I don't know what happened to him subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, earlier you made an assertion that it was Ramush Haradinaj's army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us what you understand by the expression "Ramush Haradinaj's army"? Firstly tell us that, and then I'm going to ask you some other questions about that. What is your understanding of what Ramush Haradinaj's army was or is?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramush Haradinaj was their superior. They were his troops. They were certainly not mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us if they were normal VJ members or normal MUP or SUP people at the side of the road. Can you -- do you now have any comment about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- what -- that expression you just used, "KLA," when did you first hear of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it on TV. They showed footage of them being trained in Albania and elsewhere. It was on the television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's when I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what information do you have, if any, that the people on the road, who shot at you, were Ramush Haradinaj's army? Or is that just supposition? Make it clear for the Trial Chamber, okay. We want to be clear about what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Ramush Haradinaj's army since he was their commander. He issued them -- he issued orders to them. I did not issue orders to them. It was Ramush Haradinaj personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who, Ramush?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At school. I knew him from passing, but I never spoke with him. I only know him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think you managed to make it to safety and you were hospitalised and -- I think for a period of about two months. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in hospital or after your release from hospital, did you learn of your father's disappearance?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left the hospital, I learned it then. My brother lived in Sremska Palanka. They came to visit me there, all of them, but no one would tell me what had happened. When I came to Sremska Palanka, to my brother's place, his older son Milos -- since he loved his grandfather very much and was always with him, he said, Dad, let's call grandpa. He said that a few times, and then my brother told him, You can't call him. He was taken away by the Siptars. And the son asked, Where did they catch him? And my brother said, In front of the house. I was wounded on the 25th, so that must have been on the 27th or on the 28th, and the late Vida was killed on the 30th in front of her house where the headquarters were, just across from her house. The whole house was riddled with bullets. She was over 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you relied upon information that you received from your nephew or brother to find out what had happened to your --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Later did your -- were your father's remains located?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, but classically we need to know what was the basis of the brother's information. Now, Your Honours will have seen the witness statement. MR. DI FAZIO: Sure, I can get that, that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where your brother got his information about your father's disappearance?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since my sister lived in Djakovica, she heard about that and she relayed that to my brother in Palanka. My brother didn't go there, not until his body was found, and then we -- he went there to bury him. But my sister Bosiljka was the first one to learn about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where she got her information? And I'm talking now about the circumstances -- any information about the circumstances of your father's disappearance?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A cousin of mine on my uncle's side lives in Djakovica. His neighbour was with the fire-fighting squad. I believe they went there to collect bodies, and since he had known my father, he told my cousin, They found our uncle. And he asked, Where? And then the neighbour said, At Radonjic Lake. He went to my sister's and told her that they found my late uncle -- that they found the late uncle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The witness is answering questions now about how he learnt about the discovery at the Lake Radonjic canal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's clear. I know, but I'll deal with this so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are two approaches. The first one is that you stop the witness and then focus his attention again on the attention. If, however, he's telling something that would come up later in his testimony anyhow, then it's not a major problem to let him finish the answer because then the information is there and then you can return to it. But it happened frequently that -- where the witness did not specifically answer to the question, that you did not return to that issue for reasons not always known to us. Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you questions about your father's -- the discovery of your father's remains; I'm going to ask questions about the circumstances under which he disappeared. Now, you've already told us what your brother said to you, and you've already told us that he said that -- he gave you an explanation when your nephew was there as well. You then explained that your brother got his information about how your father disappeared from your sister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not talking about your father being found in the lake or in the canal; I'm talking about how he disappeared from his home, his house, in the village. Okay. Now, where did your sister get information about how your father disappeared from his house in his village? That's all I'm asking you about, that part.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My late father was at my brother Djordje's house, since their houses were close. He went to his house to watch the news. He left his house at 8.30 p.m. After that, he wanted to go to our street where the house was, and that's where he was caught. The next day, my aunt and uncle went to his house, and they found the door closed, and they called his name but there was no reply. My uncle broke one of the windows to the bedroom and entered, and they realised that the house was empty. They went to the field, my aunt, my uncle, the late Vida, and her sister Borka, all of them. In the meantime, my cousin Miodrag Antic, he went to see the father. When he returned to Decani, since there was no telephone connection in Locane, he called my brother in Djakovica and told him that. He told him that the father had disappeared. And then the brother called my sister Bosiljka. And then Bosiljka called my brother in Sremska Palanka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question, Mr. Antic. You said: "He wanted to go to our street where the house was, and that's where he was caught." He was caught by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The neighbours. Who else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was present, as far as you know, when he was caught?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean on our side? The Serbs? Or who caught him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I just want to know: Who with his own eyes saw your father being caught?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next question is: Who then could tell you or anyone else that your father was caught at that moment, at that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My late aunt told me that; her name is Milosava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But she was not present either, was she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, she was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But she knew when he had left her house, and she knew that he disappeared that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then take it that from the fact that your father left the house and wanted to return to his own house and has disappeared since then, that you assume that on his way from the house to his own house, he must have been caught by someone? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that you have no concrete further information about who exactly at that time, who and how many people caught him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how many people there were since I didn't see it myself, but I suppose he was caught by our immediate neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you some questions about the discovery of your father's remains. Do you know when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- did you ever see your father's remains?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have a brace for my leg. I was still using my crutches, and I couldn't walk all that much. My wife and my sister, Bosiljka, went to the hotel to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What hotel is that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hotel Pastrika, in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss that episode with your wife, Jovanka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if she had any success or was able to identify anything?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't able to see the body, the remains. What was given to us were the key and the mirror that he had on him. The key belonged to him and the pipe belonged to him, and that's how we identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to ask you one question about one of those items, that's the key. Okay. Now, do your best, if you possibly could, please, to provide as much detail as you can. You said what was given to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all, I have no objection to Mr. Di Fazio leading, if this evidence is important; secondly, there is DNA evidence in this instance which is not in dispute. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. It's -- I'm just about ended by examination-in-chief, this is the last topic, if Your Honours please, and I can wrap it up in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Emmerson raises the issue whether personal belongings play any role in identification of the person where there -- I take it the DNA result is -- you agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not in dispute. Nevertheless, if you would like -- MR. DI FAZIO: I would just like this man to finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to put one or two questions but for other reasons then -- MR. DI FAZIO: I just want the witness to finish his story. That's basically what I wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- well, I will lead you on this. Your wife went to the hotel, and there she examined some personal possessions. Was there a key there that belonged to your father?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your family take the key back to your house and try it in the door and did it work?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally took the key back to the house and used it, and it worked. On the key, there was a string which he used to tie the key to his pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Antic, I'd like to thank you for answering my questions and telling your story to the Trial Chamber. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Antic, you will now be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence. Mr. Emmerson is counsel for Mr. Haradinaj. Mr. Emmerson, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Antic -- sorry, can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one or two questions, first of all, about your role as a reserve police officer. I want to read to you, if I may, just for a moment a sentence from the statement that you made to the Prosecution investigators in this case in April 2002. I think you had a chance to read that statement before coming into court. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In that statement, there is a passage which reads - and I'll read it slowly so it can be translated for you - "I was also an MUP reservist in Decani since 1990, and I was occasionally called in when tensions were rising. From the beginning of 1998 on, I was permanently operational as a reservist until I was injured on the 25th of May, 1998." This is page 2, second paragraph. Now, I'm just seeing if I can jog your memory about your own position during the early months of 1998. You seem to have said there that from the beginning of 1998, you were permanently operational as a reservist. You gave us some evidence earlier on, saying that during the first three months of 1998, you thought you were working part time in the factory and part time for the police. Can you clarify for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not true that I had worked for three months. The factory was not operating at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's very helpful. So can we say then from -- at least from January 1998, you were working full time as a police officer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since when? Which year did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: January 1998.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were there other reserve police officers in your village of Lloqan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Spasoje Mrvaljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And any others, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of, just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There were only five Serb families in the village, but as far as you can recall no other families had members in the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, again, just so that we're clear, was it possible to be a member of the reserve police if you were Albanian or only if you were Serb?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Muslims, too, were working. There's one, who was with the police, who was a Catholic. He worked in Junik. It wasn't just Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So the Muslims you're referring to, would they be Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some Albanians were in Pec but not in Decani, those who were loyal.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, active-duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And - again just to be clear - in the reserve police were there any Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just in Decani, local policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me just put the question clearly. In the reserve police, were there any Albanians, as far as you knew -- in the reserve police? Sorry, Mr. Antic, I'm not sure, are you picking up my question.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many Albanians in total are you aware of who were in the police proper; that is to say, the full-time police, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? You mean in Decani or in Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Tell us about both if you were aware, but confine your answer, please, to 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Catholic who worked with us in Decani. His name was Robert, and they killed him, too. He was from Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know of any other Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know another one from Junik. When the shooting first started, he got a rifle, a uniform, and he fled. But I forget his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you, yourself, were armed, I think. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can we be clear, were you armed with both a pistol and an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a semi-automatic rifle and a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And similarly, your colleague from the village, Spasoje - and I'll get -- correct my pronunciation if I get it wrong - Dvaljevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And would you leave your weapons behind when you left the police station, or would you take them home with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, did you understand my question clearly? When you left the police station at the end of the day to go home, did you take your weapons with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the pistol, not the rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: Do you know if there were any Serb families living a little further south from you in the village of Ponosevac during the first part of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ponosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is far from Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's south of Junik, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know. I know. Junik -- the distance between by village and Junik is 12 kilometres, and then I don't know about the distance between Junik and Ponosevac. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, leaving the distances aside, do you know whether there were any Serbs living in Ponosevac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Nobody told your family to leave Locane in Easter, did they? Nobody came up and told you you had to leave?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody told us. They just said -- neighbours told my father and uncle, It's safe for you to stay. No one will touch you. You are elderly people. We were told, or rather, they were told, but not us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So your father was given some re-assurance by neighbours; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by Mr. Di Fazio, Did any of the Albanian families leave Locane at around the same time in -- at Easter? And you said, No. But then you went on to say that when you went back to the village to visit -- sorry, let me -- if I just develop the question. You went on to say that when you went back to the village to visit your father, he told you that there were women coming from the area around Gllogjan and also other people, Albanians, that he didn't recognise. Can I ask you: What was he telling you about these women? Was he suggesting to you that they were people who were refugees?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Albanian refugees?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that was quite soon after you left your home?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was on my way to see my father before I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. There's only a month, I think, between you leaving the house in Lloqan and the incident in which you were wounded. There's only a month in between the two, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 28th of April, not a month -- a month, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: A month --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so do you agree that it was quite soon after you left that your father told you about these refugees coming into Lloqan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was it quite soon after you left Lloqan that you went back and spoke to your father when he told you that there were Albanian women who'd come to the village from the area around Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think you can confirm, can't you, that there were quite a lot of Albanian refugees who'd fled their homes from the entire area during the latter part of April and the beginning of May?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one fled any of the Albanian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought you told us just a moment ago that these women who arrived in your village were refugees fleeing from the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, refugees. Late April, that's when they arrived, or early April possibly. As for them leaving Locane, women, no, they weren't leaving. They stayed right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's forget about Lloqan for a moment. Generally around western Kosovo in Decane and south of Decane around Junik, a lot of Albanians were leaving their homes, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Junik is far away from where I was, 12 kilometres --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about that build-up and see if you can help us with it at all. All right. When the incident occurred in which you were shot, just to be clear, did you know any of the people or recognise any of the people who fired on your vehicle, as individuals?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all lost there. That moment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the latter part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see that the witness is making a gesture.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I see if I can clarify your answer. Are you saying you ducked down? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were all young men aged between 20 and 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You didn't know any of them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you don't know what villages they were from or where they might have been based?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They might have been from Ljubenic or from Glodja.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Obviously, they might have been from anywhere, but you didn't know where they were from?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think you told us that they seemed not to know how to handle their weapons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you say they looked away when they were firing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the bullets all went under the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, this incident happened on the main road, didn't it, from Peje down towards Decane?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the bus station is in Ljubenic, you pass bus station and then 100 metres on from there, there's a bend in the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We'll --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a straight stretch of the road, and they stood right beside the pylons along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We'll look at a map in a moment or two, but so that I'm clear, you were driving along the main Peje to Gjakove road when this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: On that main road, not on any side roads?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was it safe in -- on the 25th of May? Was it understood to be safe? Were your commanders telling you it was safe for vehicles to drive up and down without an armed escort?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. For a month, we couldn't take that road at all. It wasn't safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When was that month?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 25th of May and June, late June.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So until the incident in which you were injured, it had been a road that you could drive along, as far as you knew, safely?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Up until the 25th of May. Even then, it was risky.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, I just want to make absolutely sure we've all understood your evidence correctly. Prior to the incident when you were shot, before that incident, as far as you were aware, it was safe for police officers to drive in ordinary vehicles up and down the road from Peje to Decane?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In passenger vehicles, but they would do 100 kilometres per hour. It wasn't safe. It was at break-neck speed and at great risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, but there was no requirement for you to be accompanied by an armoured vehicle when travelling that road?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. The uniform that you and your colleague were wearing, would that have been a blue camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was it a camouflage uniform that the reserve police officers wore?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it was a blue one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was it blue with different colours?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue and coffee colour --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but more blue than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And with a pattern on it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no pattern really. Just a very small one, nearly invisible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. I'm going to come in just a moment to what the situation was in terms of fighting around that time, but before I do that, I want to ask you some questions about your father and the date on which he disappeared. And just to be absolutely clear about this, so that we've understood the route by which you have this information, am I right in thinking, first of all, that after you were shot on the 25th, you were taken to a military hospital in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you stayed there, I think, with your family in Serbia from the day that you, yourself, were shot until the end of July. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then at the end of July, you and your family moved back to Decane?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, again, am I right in thinking that nobody told you about your father's disappearance whilst you were still in hospital?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so the first time that you heard about it was sometime after the end of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the hospital and arrived at my brother's in Sremska Palanka. My older son asked me to call my father, his grandfather, and then my brother said, Don't call him. He was captured by the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but that incident, that conversation, took place at or after the end of July. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What? June.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. You were in hospital until the end of July in Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so that we're clear, it was after you came out of hospital and returned to Decane that that conversation took place; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not with my brother. With my wife and sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me put it to you another way, see if we can get to this a different route. Did you learn of your father's death, or rather, your father's disappearance, did you learn that your father had disappeared at any time before you left the hospital? Did you know about it before you left the hospital or only afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards, when my brother said that our father had gone missing, since my son asked to speak to his granddad.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I understand. Now, again, so that we've got the sequence accurate, your aunt and uncle are called Djordje and Milosava, and they live in Lloqan or lived in Lloqan at the time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because I think the translation came over earlier on in a slightly inaccurate form. I think Djordje is your father's brother? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, brother. And Milosava is Djordje's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And again, so that we're clear, as far as you understand the sequence of the information passing along, is it right that your cousin Miodrag went and spoke to your aunt and uncle Djordje and Milosava?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And as far as you understood it, they told your cousin Miodrag that your father had been to their house -- had been to their house and had left, and the following morning they looked for him and his house was still locked; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was locked. Then the uncle broke the window to enter the house. He broke the door down as well, and they did not find him. His shoes were not there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand. I'm trying to understand the sequence by which the information came to you. Now, Miodrag spoke to Djordje and Milosava and then I think you told us that, when Miodrag came back to Decane, he told one of your brothers, who told your sister, who then told your other brother. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. When Miodrag came back from Locane, when he heard that my father had gone missing, he came to Decani. Then he called up my brother, and then my brother went to see our sister and he told her.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you have only one brother or did you at the time only have one brother?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had. He died a month ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, though, Mr. Antic. I thought you told us, earlier on, that your cousin Miodrag told one of your brothers, who then told your sister, who then told the brother, who told you. Is that right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sister told my brother in Sremska Palanka, but that brother passed away.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She called him and he was the only brother I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the brother in Sremska Palanka is the one who told you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry for this rather lengthy examination of that aspect of the matter, but it's quite important to know in terms of how close the information you've got was to the original source. Now, Djordje and Milosava, your aunt and uncle, died, I think, of natural causes in 2001, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: How sure are you of the date that you've given us? Because you've told us that your father went missing on the 28th of May. Can you help us -- just pause for a moment. Can you help us. When you say the 28th, do you mean the night of the 27th to the 28th or the night of the 28th to the 29th?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The night of the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So does that mean going into the 29th?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I mean, do you think it's possible there could be an error by a day or two either way, in that date?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I think the date is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: About 20 minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we first should have a break. Mr. Di Fazio, could you -- first of all, could other Defence counsel give an impression on how much time they would need? Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll be very short, if at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'll be shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Di Fazio, do you have already any impression on whether and -- MR. DI FAZIO: So far, no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Antic, we'll have a break. We'll have a break and we'll resume at a quarter to 5.00. May I invite Defence counsel to focus on - during the break - on a letter they, I expect, have received by now. It must be rather recent letter because it refers to what happened at 3.00 p.m. this afternoon and to see -- to consider whether there's any objection against the proposed course to take -- as proposed by the Prosecution. Yes. We'll then hear from you. We have a break and we'll resume at a quarter to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I invited Defence counsel to look at the letter. Just to briefly introduce the matter, we have two requests; one is for protective measures, the other is for a postponement of the start of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the fact that a request for protective measures is still pending, I would like to invite you if you respond - I don't know whether you're going to respond on behalf of all Defence counsel - but to keep in mind the -- that protective measures are still pending. So I leave the postponement. The Chamber has read the request for postponement at the start of Witness 8 and is, therefore, aware of the reasons given. If you can deal with it without going into private session, fine, we'd like to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Two things, if I may. We've responded in writing already in relation to the protective measures application --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've -- the Chamber has --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- has seen that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and perhaps it's good to have that on the record. The Chamber has invited the parties to give its first reaction, and this has been sent to the Legal Officer of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's good to have this be clearly on the record. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely clear, is Your Honour asking me to respond at the moment in relation to the postponement issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only because the other matter is pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that it's pending. Exactly so. What I need to inform Your Honours of factually are three things: First of all, the name and telephone number that appear on the document concerned, that document was handed to the Prosecution in the form of investigator Kelly by the Witness 8 in November 2005. The relevant passage, if I can just read it to you, from the witness's own statement in relation to that document reads as follows, and I'll delete as appropriate: "On the reverse side of this paper it states ...," and then the name and telephone number that are recorded there appear, and the statement goes on: "... which is the name and telephone contact number of the person who has all the refugees' records." In other words, the Prosecution were aware from November 2005 what the significance of that document was. The letter indicates that at 3.00 this afternoon, with the witness being due to testify later in the afternoon, on closer examination it was noted that the name and telephone number is there recorded. With the greatest of respect, that is an extremely surprising way to put it, given that it was clear in a November 2005 statement what that document was and what the telephone number was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would have preferred after one year and a half studying the document, we noticed that. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm surprised that it's closer inspection of a document that was clearly very closely inspected in November 2005, that's a rather strange way of putting it. But the letter goes on to indicate that investigator Kelly has made contact with the person whose name and telephone number appeared on that document, and describes the organisation for which the person works. And then goes on to say that that individual has a statement in his possession made in August 1999 from Witness 8, and that the person concerned is also aware that Witness 8 has provided the Humanitarian Law Centre with a statement. And the Office of the Prosecutor says it cannot obtain either statement, it appears, today and it can only be faxed tomorrow. Well, of course, the witness will still be in the witness box tomorrow. It goes on: "The statement may contain evidence relevant to the witness's testimony" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I perhaps put one question in between. Do we know what language the statement still to be faxed is, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can make the inquiry, but I can't tell you right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And there's then a promise to make a relevant inquiry with the Humanitarian Law Centre. Once again, a rather surprising suggestion, because if the author of this letter had turned their attention to the statement of Witness 728, that is the outstanding Humanitarian Law Centre witness, Your Honours will remember we had one, the very first witness, and another who was postponed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The author of this letter would have discovered that the statement concerned is appended to the statement of Witness 728 and summarised in the body of the statement. It is, in fact, an unsigned version of a statement made by Witness 8 to the MUP on the 24th of December, 2001. We have a signed version of that statement, which has been recovered from the Prosecution's material. So, so far as the Humanitarian Law Centre is concerned, the Prosecution already has both the original signed MUP statement and the unsigned version that was handed by the MUP to Witness 728. They are the same document, and they exist both in their original Serbian language and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So in our submission, the appropriate course is to proceed with this witness's testimony. No doubt Mr. -- the person whose name appears on the document can be encouraged to make sure that the statement is faxed as early as possible tomorrow. If it's not possible to conclude the witness's testimony during the course of the day tomorrow or if it's necessary to have him re-called to deal with that statement, then that can be done. But may I make it clear, and as the Prosecution themselves are well aware and Your Honours will be aware when you read the statements and proofing notes of this witness, there are already seven sets of witness instructions or statements in existence for this witness which are in themselves wholly and in many respects inconsistent with one another. Yet another statement from him is unlikely to significantly alter the course of examination-in-chief or cross-examination, and if it does there is no reason why the witness cannot be either held over in cross-examination until after the break or, indeed, re-called to deal with it. The alternative would be to call the witness whose number, I believe, is 21, who is in The Hague, and in respect of whom the Defence, certainly so far as I am concerned, are quite unable to deal with that witness's evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but apart from whether you are able to deal with that. Mr. Re, if we would follow your suggestion, could we continue after the present witness with Witness 21 today? We've still got two hours left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could we continue -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness at present, I expect, that altogether that we would finish with the witness in 30, 40 minutes, and then of course we could start with the next witness. Would Witness 21 be available?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness 21 is not available today; he is only available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson, please proceed, I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should simply emphasise that I made it clear on Monday to Mr. Re that preparation this week would be severely hampered by any changes in the witness order, because both Witness 8 and Witness 21 require a very, very considerable amount of out-of-court preparation. As the week has progressed, it has become quite clear that it was the Prosecution's intention to call Witness 8 and to call him today. We're simply not in a position to deal with the evidence of Witness 21 in any form, and as I understand it from Mr. Dutertre, he does not expect that Witness 21's testimony could be concluded within one day, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Re, let's first, for procedural reasons, because we are discussing at this moment something which is not on the record in any way. The Prosecution is invited to file confidentially this letter, which is a kind of a request letter, and let's not be more formal than -- the Chamber will consider the letter as a request for postponement of the start of the testimony of Witness 8, so that we have at least the letter later on the record. We all have it in front of us. Would you please respond to -- but I should first -- I had no answer yet, Mr. Emmerson, on whether you spoke on behalf of all Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I join in the remarks made by Mr. Emmerson with regard to both Witness 8 and Witness 21. Witness 21 is a witness who I have indicated some time ago would be a long witness with regard to my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I also join in those remarks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Re, would you please briefly respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The reason why I wrote a letter was because I could not have filed an application in the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- and it was just to alert the Chamber and the parties to our application foreshadowed. The application is put mainly on the basis of the apparent 1999 statement which was basically brought to the attention of Mr. Kearney, who is the lawyer who is taking the witness around 3.00 this afternoon, upon closer review and reflection upon what was actually contained in the witness's notes. I've set out in the letter that Mr. Kearney made the connection yesterday in proofing the witness when that name, which is in the letter, was -- the full name -- the witness gave Mr. Kearney the full name yesterday, but only one part of the name, the person's given name, is actually in the note which is attached to the statement. And as unfortunate as it is, it wasn't until a lawyer was reviewing it in some depth in talking to the witness again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
